packs.title: Hills, Art & Shores
packs.promise: Follow a hill artwork, conservation stories, a changing gallery and the shores beyond the town centre.

q.s: Connect wildlife interpretation with practical conservation work.
st: Arrange or present valid admission with the applicable fee, discount or eligible free entry. Normal adult 16+ admission is currently NZ$68 before fees; confirm age-five pricing and any caregiver or SuperGold procedure with Guest Services. Children 15 and under must be with a responsible adult.

Use the signed Brecon Street visitor entrance around 13:15–13:30; the park is closed Christmas Day. Arrive at least 15 minutes before any encounter you choose. Follow open visitor paths and keep phones and cameras away inside the Kiwi House; stay quiet near animals. For limited mobility, check the steep gravel paths and mandatory Kiwi House hills with the park before visiting.

Choose three species represented in readable labels, the audio guide outside the Kiwi House or a keeper presentation. For each, record its supplied name and one conservation action actually described. An animal does not need to appear or perform.
Write your three species-and-action pairs after leaving any no-phone or quiet area. Mark which source supplied each action; do not turn a guess about an animal into a conservation claim.

q.s: Give a current gallery work four different kinds of attention.
st: Check that a free exhibition is open, then enter the ground-floor visitor entrance at Dart House from the lower carpark around noon. Observe current staff instructions; no ticketed workshop or purchase is needed.

Choose one displayed work with readable interpretation. Divide a page or note into four boxes: supplied fact, visible detail, personal response and question. Write after leaving the room if staff restrict note-taking there.

Fill the first box with one fact from the label or interpretation, the second with something you can see, the third with your own response and the last with a question. Keep the artist’s stated information separate from your invention.
Give your four-box piece a short title of your own. Record the work’s displayed name or another clear identification so your response stays connected to this exhibition.

q.s: Build a small lakescape from colours, edges and distance.
st: At the St Omer Park turnaround, choose a safe dry public lakefront position, away from the water edge, play equipment and boat-working areas. Do this before retracing the public pavements.
Make three horizontal bands on a page, or write three short lines: near shore, water and far distance. Give each one a colour, texture or edge you can actually see today.
Connect the bands with one sentence about how the distance changes. If cloud hides the far peaks, use the visible horizon or cloud edge instead of inventing a clear view.
Give your lakescape a short title of your own. Then return by the same open Lake Esplanade and Beach Street pavements and finish the Transit proof back at the town start.

packs.title: Town & Gardens
packs.promise: Read a library corner, a lakefront cottage and the Gardens through close observation and small acts of making.

q.s: Collect the clues that survive on a former library’s street face.
st: Stand on an open public pavement at the Stanley and Ballarat Street corner, outside the former Library and Reading Room. Keep doorways clear; do not enter the private property.
Collect three visible building clues: one surface texture, one opening shape and one facade detail. Use an actual inscription only if it is readable; otherwise choose another visible detail.
For each clue, write where it appears so someone else could find it from the street. Separate what you observed from the former-library identity supplied by the heritage record.
Choose the clue that would best help someone recognize this particular corner. Then follow Ballarat Street toward the pedestrian Mall on public pavement.

q.s: Make a wide view and a close detail tell one small story.
st: Find the named cottage at Marine Parade and Earl Street from the public pavement. Keep outside the private property and leave its entrance clear.
Choose a wide view showing the cottage’s outline and one close detail visible from that same public position, such as an edge, opening or surface.
Make a two-panel sketch or write two short captions: one for the whole building and one for your chosen detail. Use your own observations, without inventing a resident’s story.
Add one sentence explaining how the close detail changes the wider view. Finish this afternoon at the public corner; shopping is optional.

q.s: Collect how stone, planting and a bridge meet the same water.
st: Follow the open main avenue back to the pond area and use public paths to find a view of the stone bridge. Stay behind the water edge; a map pin does not require standing on a planted bank or in water.
Collect three ways the pond meets its surroundings: one built edge, one planted edge and the bridge’s position relative to the water.
Locate each clue in words. If reflections are visible, you may use one as an extra detail, but do not depend on still water, wildlife or a running fountain.
Choose which edge most changes the pond’s shape in your view. Write why, then return by an open public path to Marine Parade outside the Bathhouse.
